notes:
1. Basic Facts
  • A mineral is a naturally occurring inorganic substance with a definite chemical composition and characteristic physical properties.
  • Mineral resources are naturally occurring concentrations of minerals that can be economically extracted and used.
  • Minerals are essential raw materials for:
  • Industry.
  • Construction.
  • Transport.
  • Energy.
  • Electronics.
  • Agriculture.
  • Most mineral resources are non-renewable on the human timescale.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Minerals → Exhaustible / Non-Renewable Resources

2. Ore
  • An ore is a naturally occurring mineral deposit from which one or more useful substances can be extracted economically.
  • Every ore contains a useful mineral, but every mineral deposit is not necessarily an ore.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Mineral ≠ Ore

Ore → Economically Extractable Mineral Deposit

3. Gangue
  • Gangue refers to unwanted or commercially valueless material associated with an ore.
  • Gangue must often be removed during mineral processing.
4. Mineral Deposit
  • A mineral deposit is a natural concentration of minerals in Earth's crust.
  • It becomes an economic resource only when extraction is technically and financially feasible.
5. Factors Determining Economic Value

Mineral extraction depends on:

  • Grade of ore.
  • Quantity of deposit.
  • Depth.
  • Accessibility.
  • Technology.
  • Transport cost.
  • Market price.
  • Environmental restrictions.
6. Ore Grade
  • Ore grade refers to the concentration of the useful mineral or metal in the ore.
  • Higher-grade deposits generally contain a greater proportion of the desired substance.
7. Classification of Minerals

Minerals may broadly be grouped into:

  • Metallic minerals.
  • Non-metallic minerals.
  • Energy minerals.
8. Metallic Minerals

Metallic minerals contain metals that can be extracted.

They are broadly divided into:

  • Ferrous minerals.
  • Non-ferrous minerals.
  • Precious metals.
9. Ferrous Minerals
  • Ferrous minerals contain iron or are closely associated with the iron and steel industry.

Important examples:

  • Iron ore.
  • Manganese.
  • Chromite.
📌 Must-Memorise

Ferrous → Iron-Related Minerals

10. Non-Ferrous Minerals

Important non-ferrous minerals include:

  • Copper.
  • Bauxite/aluminium ore.
  • Lead.
  • Zinc.
  • Tin.
11. Precious Metals

Examples include:

  • Gold.
  • Silver.
  • Platinum-group metals.
12. Non-Metallic Minerals

Important non-metallic minerals include:

  • Limestone.
  • Mica.
  • Gypsum.
  • Dolomite.
  • Phosphorite.
  • Magnesite.
  • Graphite.
  • Salt.
13. Energy Minerals

Important energy minerals include:

  • Coal.
  • Lignite.
  • Petroleum.
  • Natural gas.
  • Uranium.
  • Thorium.

Energy resources are treated in greater detail in the next chapter.

14. Geological Distribution of Minerals
  • Minerals are unevenly distributed because different geological processes create different deposits.
  • Peninsular India is particularly rich in metallic minerals.
  • Sedimentary basins contain major coal, petroleum and limestone resources.
  • Coastal sands contain important heavy minerals.
15. Peninsular Plateau — Mineral Storehouse
  • Ancient crystalline rocks of Peninsular India contain large deposits of metallic minerals.
  • Major mineral-rich regions include:
  • Chotanagpur Plateau.
  • Odisha Plateau.
  • Chhattisgarh.
  • Karnataka Plateau.
  • Parts of Maharashtra.
  • Parts of Tamil Nadu.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Peninsular Plateau → Major Mineral Belt

16. Mineral Belts of India

Major mineral belts are commonly identified as:

  • Northeastern Peninsular Belt.
  • Southwestern Peninsular Belt.
  • Northwestern Belt.
  • Himalayan Belt in selected minerals.
17. Northeastern Peninsular Mineral Belt

This belt includes parts of:

  • Jharkhand.
  • Odisha.
  • Chhattisgarh.
  • West Bengal.

It is rich in:

  • Coal.
  • Iron ore.
  • Manganese.
  • Bauxite.
  • Mica.
  • Limestone.
18. Chotanagpur Plateau
  • Chotanagpur Plateau is one of India's most important mineral regions.
  • It contains:
  • Coal.
  • Iron ore.
  • Mica.
  • Bauxite.
  • Copper.
  • Limestone.
📌 Must-Memorise

Chotanagpur → Mineral Heartland of India

19. Southwestern Mineral Belt

This belt includes parts of:

  • Karnataka.
  • Goa.
  • Maharashtra.
  • Tamil Nadu.

Important minerals include:

  • Iron ore.
  • Manganese.
  • Bauxite.
  • Gold.
  • Limestone.
20. Northwestern Mineral Belt

This belt includes:

  • Rajasthan.
  • Gujarat and adjoining regions.

Important minerals include:

  • Copper.
  • Zinc.
  • Lead.
  • Gypsum.
  • Limestone.
  • Marble.
  • Rock phosphate.
  • Petroleum and natural gas in sedimentary basins.
21. Iron Ore — Importance
  • Iron ore is the basic raw material of the iron and steel industry.
  • It is essential for:
  • Machinery.
  • Railways.
  • Automobiles.
  • Construction.
  • Engineering industries.
22. Major Types of Iron Ore

Important iron ores include:

  • Magnetite.
  • Hematite.
  • Limonite.
  • Siderite.
📌 TNPSC Favourite

Iron Ore Types → Magnetite + Hematite

23. Magnetite
  • Magnetite has the chemical formula Fe₃O₄.
  • It has a high iron content.
  • It is magnetic.
  • It is generally considered a high-grade iron ore.
📌 Must-Memorise

Magnetite → Fe₃O₄ → Magnetic

24. Hematite
  • Hematite has the chemical formula Fe₂O₃.
  • It is one of the most important iron ores used commercially in India.
  • It is commonly reddish or brownish.
📌 Must-Memorise

Hematite → Fe₂O₃

25. Limonite
  • Limonite is a hydrated iron oxide material.
  • It generally contains less iron than magnetite and good-quality hematite.
26. Siderite
  • Siderite is iron carbonate.
  • Its chemical formula is FeCO₃.
  • It is generally less important commercially in India.
27. Major Iron Ore Belts

Important iron-ore regions include:

  • Odisha-Jharkhand belt.
  • Durg-Bastar-Chandrapur belt.
  • Karnataka belt.
  • Goa-Maharashtra belt.
28. Odisha-Jharkhand Iron Belt

Important areas include:

  • Keonjhar.
  • Mayurbhanj.
  • Sundargarh.
  • Singhbhum.

The region contains high-quality hematite deposits.

29. Noamundi
  • Noamundi is an important iron-ore mining area in Jharkhand.
  • It lies in the Singhbhum mineral belt.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Noamundi → Iron Ore → Jharkhand

30. Singhbhum
  • Singhbhum region of Jharkhand is rich in:
  • Iron ore.
  • Copper.
  • Other metallic minerals.
31. Keonjhar
  • Keonjhar district of Odisha is an important iron-ore producing region.
  • It forms part of the Odisha-Jharkhand mineral belt.
32. Mayurbhanj
  • Mayurbhanj in Odisha is historically important for iron-ore deposits.
  • The Badampahar region is well known.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Badampahar → Iron Ore → Odisha

33. Durg-Bastar-Chandrapur Belt
  • This mineral belt extends across parts of Chhattisgarh and Maharashtra.
  • It contains major iron-ore deposits.
34. Bailadila Hills
  • Bailadila Hills lie in the Bastar region of Chhattisgarh.
  • They contain high-grade hematite iron ore.
  • Bailadila means "hump of an ox" because of the shape of the hills.
📌 Must-Memorise

Bailadila → Iron Ore → Chhattisgarh

35. Dalli-Rajhara
  • Dalli-Rajhara in Chhattisgarh is an important iron-ore mining region.
  • It historically supplied iron ore to the Bhilai Steel Plant.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Dalli-Rajhara → Bhilai Steel Plant

36. Karnataka Iron Ore Belt

Important iron-ore regions include:

  • Ballari/Bellary.
  • Chitradurga.
  • Chikkamagaluru.
  • Tumakuru.
37. Kudremukh
  • Kudremukh lies in Karnataka.
  • It is historically associated with magnetite iron ore.
  • The name means "horse face," referring to the shape of a mountain peak.
📌 Must-Memorise

Kudremukh → Magnetite → Karnataka

38. Ballari Region
  • Ballari region of Karnataka is rich in iron ore.
  • It is part of the mineral-rich eastern Karnataka plateau.
39. Goa Iron Ore
  • Goa contains important iron-ore deposits.
  • Its location near the Arabian Sea historically favoured mineral exports through ports.
40. Iron Ore and Steel Plants

Important spatial relationships include:

  • Iron ore mines.
  • Coalfields.
  • Limestone deposits.
  • Railways.
  • Water sources.

These factors influenced the location of steel plants.

41. Manganese — Importance
  • Manganese is an important ferrous mineral.
  • It is used mainly in steel production.
  • It improves:
  • Hardness.
  • Strength.
  • Resistance of steel.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Manganese → Steel Alloy

42. Other Uses of Manganese

Manganese is also used in:

  • Batteries.
  • Chemicals.
  • Glass.
  • Paints.
43. Manganese Distribution

Important manganese-bearing regions occur in:

  • Odisha.
  • Karnataka.
  • Maharashtra.
  • Madhya Pradesh.
  • Goa.
  • Andhra Pradesh.
44. Balaghat
  • Balaghat in Madhya Pradesh is an important manganese-mining region.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Balaghat → Manganese → Madhya Pradesh

45. Manganese in Karnataka

Important deposits occur around:

  • Ballari.
  • Chitradurga.
  • Shivamogga and adjoining belts.
46. Chromite
  • Chromite is the principal ore of chromium.
  • Chromium is used in:
  • Stainless steel.
  • Alloy steel.
  • Refractory materials.
  • Chromite is a strategically important mineral.
47. Chromite Formula
  • Chromite is broadly represented by FeCr₂O₄.
48. Sukinda Valley
  • Sukinda Valley in Odisha is one of India's most important chromite-bearing regions.
📌 Must-Memorise

Sukinda → Chromite → Odisha

49. Chromium and Stainless Steel
  • Chromium increases corrosion resistance.
  • It is a major component of stainless steel.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Chromium → Stainless Steel

50. Bauxite — Basic Facts
  • Bauxite is the principal ore of aluminium.
  • It forms mainly through intense weathering and leaching of aluminium-rich rocks.
  • It is commonly associated with lateritic conditions.
📌 Must-Memorise

Bauxite → Aluminium Ore

51. Composition of Bauxite
  • Bauxite contains hydrated aluminium oxides along with impurities such as iron oxides and silica.
  • It is not a single pure mineral.
52. Aluminium — Importance

Aluminium is:

  • Light.
  • Corrosion resistant.
  • Good conductor.
  • Malleable.

It is used in:

  • Aircraft.
  • Transport.
  • Electrical equipment.
  • Packaging.
  • Construction.
53. Bauxite Distribution

Major bauxite-bearing regions occur in:

  • Odisha.
  • Chhattisgarh.
  • Jharkhand.
  • Maharashtra.
  • Gujarat.
  • Madhya Pradesh.
  • Andhra Pradesh.
54. Koraput Bauxite
  • Koraput district and adjoining plateau regions of Odisha contain major bauxite deposits.
  • Panchpatmali is an important bauxite-mining area.
📌 Must-Memorise

Panchpatmali → Bauxite → Odisha

55. Bauxite and Laterite
  • Bauxite often develops in tropical regions through prolonged chemical weathering and leaching.
  • Therefore, it is commonly associated with lateritic plateaus.
56. Aluminium Extraction
  • Bauxite is refined to produce alumina.
  • Alumina is then electrolytically reduced to aluminium.
  • Aluminium production requires large quantities of electricity.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Aluminium Industry → Highly Electricity Intensive

57. Copper — Importance

Copper is important because it is:

  • An excellent conductor of electricity.
  • Ductile.
  • Malleable.
  • Resistant to corrosion.

It is widely used in:

  • Electrical wiring.
  • Electronics.
  • Alloys.
  • Machinery.
58. Major Copper Regions

Important copper deposits occur in:

  • Rajasthan.
  • Madhya Pradesh.
  • Jharkhand.
59. Khetri Copper Belt
  • Khetri lies in Rajasthan.
  • It is one of India's best-known copper-mining regions.
  • It forms part of the Aravalli mineral belt.
📌 Must-Memorise

Khetri → Copper → Rajasthan

60. Malanjkhand
  • Malanjkhand in Madhya Pradesh is an important copper-mining area.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Malanjkhand → Copper → Madhya Pradesh

61. Singhbhum Copper Belt
  • Singhbhum in Jharkhand contains important copper deposits.
  • Ghatsila is historically associated with copper mining and processing.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Ghatsila → Copper → Jharkhand

62. Copper Alloys

Important copper alloys include:

  • Brass → Copper + Zinc.
  • Bronze → Copper + Tin.
📌 Must-Memorise

Brass → Cu + Zn

Bronze → Cu + Sn

63. Zinc
  • Zinc is a non-ferrous metal.
  • It is widely used for galvanising iron and steel.
  • Galvanisation protects metal from corrosion.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Zinc → Galvanisation

64. Lead
  • Lead is a dense metal.
  • It is used in:
  • Batteries.
  • Radiation shielding.
  • Alloys.
  • Because of toxicity, many traditional uses are increasingly restricted.
65. Lead-Zinc Belt of Rajasthan
  • Rajasthan contains major lead-zinc deposits.
  • Important mining regions include:
  • Zawar.
  • Rampura Agucha.
  • Rajpura-Dariba.
📌 Must-Memorise

Zawar → Lead-Zinc → Rajasthan

66. Zawar Mines
  • Zawar lies near Udaipur in Rajasthan.
  • It is historically important for zinc and lead mining.
67. Rampura Agucha
  • Rampura Agucha in Rajasthan is a major lead-zinc deposit.
68. Tin
  • Tin is used in:
  • Alloys.
  • Solder.
  • Coating.
  • Cassiterite is the principal ore of tin.
📌 Must-Memorise

Tin Ore → Cassiterite

69. Cassiterite
  • Cassiterite has the chemical formula SnO₂.
  • Important Indian tin-bearing deposits occur in the Bastar region of Chhattisgarh.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Tin/Cassiterite → Chhattisgarh

70. Gold — Basic Facts
  • Gold is a precious metal.
  • It occurs in:
  • Quartz veins.
  • Lode deposits.
  • Alluvial deposits.
  • It is used in jewellery, finance, electronics and specialised industries.
71. Karnataka and Gold
  • Karnataka has historically been India's most famous gold-mining region.
  • Important gold fields include:
  • Kolar Gold Fields.
  • Hutti Gold Mines.
72. Kolar Gold Fields
  • Kolar Gold Fields, commonly called KGF, lie in Karnataka.
  • They were historically one of India's most famous gold-mining areas.
  • Large-scale mining there has ceased.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

KGF → Gold → Karnataka

73. Hutti Gold Mines
  • Hutti lies in Karnataka.
  • It is an important gold-mining region.
📌 Must-Memorise

Hutti → Gold → Karnataka

74. Gold in Quartz Veins
  • Much primary gold occurs in veins associated with ancient metamorphic and igneous rocks.
  • Weathering can release gold into river sediments.
75. Silver
  • Silver may occur with:
  • Lead.
  • Zinc.
  • Copper ores.
  • It is often recovered as a by-product rather than from independent silver mines.
76. Mica — Basic Facts
  • Mica is a non-metallic mineral.
  • It splits easily into very thin sheets.
  • It has excellent:
  • Electrical insulation.
  • Heat resistance.
  • It has been important in electrical and electronic industries.
77. Important Mica Types

Important varieties include:

  • Muscovite.
  • Biotite.
  • Phlogopite.
78. Mica Distribution

Traditional mica-producing belts include:

  • Jharkhand-Bihar belt.
  • Andhra Pradesh belt.
  • Rajasthan belt.
79. Koderma Mica Belt
  • Koderma in Jharkhand is historically famous for mica deposits.
  • It forms part of the Jharkhand-Bihar mica belt.
📌 Must-Memorise

Koderma → Mica → Jharkhand

80. Andhra Pradesh Mica Belt
  • Nellore region of Andhra Pradesh is historically associated with mica deposits.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Nellore → Mica → Andhra Pradesh

81. Limestone
  • Limestone is a sedimentary rock rich in calcium carbonate.
  • It is one of India's most important industrial minerals.
  • It is the principal raw material for cement production.
📌 Must-Memorise

Limestone → Cement

82. Other Uses of Limestone

Limestone is used in:

  • Iron and steel industry.
  • Chemical industry.
  • Building materials.
  • Lime production.
83. Limestone Distribution

Important limestone regions occur in:

  • Rajasthan.
  • Madhya Pradesh.
  • Chhattisgarh.
  • Andhra Pradesh.
  • Telangana.
  • Tamil Nadu.
  • Gujarat.
  • Karnataka.
84. Cement Industry and Limestone
  • Cement plants are often located near limestone deposits because limestone is bulky and costly to transport over long distances.
85. Dolomite
  • Dolomite is a carbonate mineral containing calcium and magnesium.
  • It is used in:
  • Iron and steel.
  • Refractories.
  • Construction.
86. Dolomite Formula
  • Dolomite has the chemical formula CaMg(CO₃)₂.
87. Gypsum
  • Gypsum is a soft sulphate mineral.
  • It is used in:
  • Cement.
  • Plaster of Paris.
  • Fertilisers.
  • Construction.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Gypsum → Cement + Plaster

88. Rajasthan and Gypsum
  • Rajasthan contains important gypsum deposits.
  • Dry climatic conditions favour evaporite mineral formation.
89. Plaster of Paris
  • Plaster of Paris is produced by partial heating of gypsum.
  • It is used for casts, moulds and construction.
90. Phosphorite / Rock Phosphate
  • Rock phosphate is an important source of phosphorus.
  • It is used in phosphate fertiliser production.
📌 Must-Memorise

Rock Phosphate → Fertiliser

91. Rajasthan Rock Phosphate
  • Rajasthan contains important rock-phosphate deposits.
  • Jhamarkotra near Udaipur is a well-known deposit.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Jhamarkotra → Rock Phosphate → Rajasthan

92. Magnesite
  • Magnesite is a magnesium carbonate mineral.
  • Its formula is MgCO₃.
  • It is used in refractory materials and magnesium industries.
93. Magnesite in Tamil Nadu
  • Tamil Nadu has important magnesite deposits around Salem.
  • The Chalk Hills near Salem are well known for magnesite.
📌 Tamil Nadu Must-Memorise

Salem → Magnesite

94. Graphite
  • Graphite is a crystalline form of carbon.
  • It is soft and electrically conductive.
  • It is used in:
  • Electrodes.
  • Batteries.
  • Lubricants.
  • Refractories.
  • Pencils.
95. Diamond
  • Diamond is a crystalline form of carbon.
  • It is the hardest naturally occurring mineral.
  • It is valued as:
  • Gemstone.
  • Industrial cutting and abrasive material.
96. Panna Diamonds
  • Panna district in Madhya Pradesh is India's most famous traditional diamond-mining region.
📌 Must-Memorise

Panna → Diamond → Madhya Pradesh

97. Kimberlite
  • Diamonds are commonly associated with kimberlite and related igneous rocks.
  • They may also occur in secondary alluvial deposits.
98. Marble
  • Marble is a metamorphic rock formed mainly from limestone.
  • It is widely used as a building and decorative stone.
99. Makrana Marble
  • Makrana in Rajasthan is famous for high-quality marble.
  • Makrana marble was used in several major historical monuments.
📌 Must-Memorise

Makrana → Marble → Rajasthan

100. Granite
  • Granite is an intrusive igneous rock.
  • It is used extensively as:
  • Building stone.
  • Flooring.
  • Decorative stone.
  • South India contains important granite resources.
101. Granite in Tamil Nadu
  • Tamil Nadu contains significant granite-bearing regions.
  • Granite quarrying occurs in several districts.
  • Quarrying requires environmental management because of land and groundwater impacts.
102. Salt

Salt is obtained from:

  • Seawater.
  • Saline lakes.
  • Brines.
  • Rock-salt deposits.
103. Coastal Salt Production

Important coastal salt-producing areas occur in:

  • Gujarat.
  • Tamil Nadu.
  • Rajasthan inland saline regions also produce salt.
104. Tamil Nadu Salt Production
  • Thoothukudi is especially important for salt pans.
  • High evaporation and coastal conditions favour salt production.
📌 Tamil Nadu Must-Memorise

Thoothukudi → Salt Pans

105. Heavy Mineral Sands

Coastal sands can contain:

  • Ilmenite.
  • Rutile.
  • Monazite.
  • Zircon.
  • Garnet.
  • Sillimanite.
📌 Must-Memorise

Beach Sands → Heavy Minerals

106. Ilmenite
  • Ilmenite is an important titanium-bearing mineral.
  • Its approximate formula is FeTiO₃.
  • It is abundant in selected coastal placer deposits.
107. Rutile
  • Rutile is a titanium dioxide mineral.
  • Its formula is TiO₂.
  • It is an important titanium ore.
108. Monazite
  • Monazite is a phosphate mineral containing rare-earth elements.
  • It can also contain thorium.
  • It is an important heavy mineral of India's coastal sands.
📌 Must-Memorise

Monazite → Thorium + Rare Earths

109. Zircon
  • Zircon is a zirconium silicate mineral.
  • It occurs in heavy-mineral beach sands.
  • It has industrial uses in ceramics and refractory materials.
110. Garnet
  • Garnet occurs in some coastal placer deposits.
  • It is used as an industrial abrasive.
111. Placer Deposit
  • A placer deposit forms when heavy resistant minerals become concentrated by flowing water, waves or currents.
  • Gold and heavy beach-sand minerals may occur in placer deposits.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Placer → Heavy Minerals Concentrated by Water

112. Beach Mineral Sands of India

Important coastal stretches occur in:

  • Kerala.
  • Tamil Nadu.
  • Odisha.
  • Andhra Pradesh.
113. Tamil Nadu Beach Minerals

Important coastal mineral-sand areas occur along parts of:

  • Kanyakumari.
  • Tirunelveli.
  • Thoothukudi.
  • Other southeastern coastal stretches.

They may contain:

  • Ilmenite.
  • Garnet.
  • Monazite.
  • Zircon.
  • Rutile.
🔗 Tamil Nadu Key Link

Southern TN Coast → Heavy Mineral Sands

114. Rare Earth Elements
  • Rare earth elements are a group of chemically similar metallic elements.
  • They are important in:
  • Electronics.
  • Magnets.
  • Renewable-energy technologies.
  • Defence applications.
  • Monazite is an important rare-earth-bearing mineral.
115. Thorium
  • Thorium is a radioactive element.
  • India's monazite-rich coastal sands are an important thorium resource.
  • Thorium is relevant to India's long-term nuclear-energy strategy.
116. Uranium
  • Uranium is a radioactive metallic element used as nuclear fuel.
  • Important Indian uranium occurrences are found in several geological belts.
117. Jaduguda
  • Jaduguda in Jharkhand is historically one of India's best-known uranium-mining areas.
📌 Must-Memorise

Jaduguda → Uranium → Jharkhand

118. Tummalapalle
  • Tummalapalle in Andhra Pradesh is an important uranium-bearing region.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Tummalapalle → Uranium → Andhra Pradesh

119. Atomic Minerals

Important atomic minerals include:

  • Uranium minerals.
  • Thorium-bearing monazite.
  • Certain rare-earth minerals.
120. Mineral Conservation

Minerals require conservation because:

  • They are finite.
  • Deposits take geological time to form.
  • Mining can damage ecosystems.
  • High-grade ores become depleted.
121. Methods of Mineral Conservation

Important measures include:

  • Efficient extraction.
  • Reducing mining waste.
  • Recycling.
  • Reusing metals.
  • Substituting scarce minerals.
  • Beneficiating low-grade ores.
122. Beneficiation
  • Beneficiation means improving the quality of ore by removing gangue and concentrating useful minerals.
  • It increases the economic value of low-grade ore.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Beneficiation → Ore Concentration

123. Mineral Recycling

Highly recyclable metals include:

  • Iron and steel.
  • Aluminium.
  • Copper.
  • Lead.

Recycling reduces the need for fresh mining.

124. Aluminium Recycling
  • Recycling aluminium requires much less energy than producing primary aluminium from bauxite.
  • Therefore, recycling has major energy and environmental benefits.
125. Mining Methods

Major mining methods include:

  • Open-cast mining.
  • Underground mining.
  • Quarrying.
  • Placer mining.
126. Open-Cast Mining
  • Open-cast mining removes overlying material to access shallow deposits.
  • It is used where minerals occur close to the surface.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Open-Cast → Shallow Deposits

127. Underground Mining
  • Underground mining uses shafts and tunnels to reach deeper deposits.
  • It is more technically complex and hazardous.
128. Quarrying
  • Quarrying is commonly used to extract:
  • Limestone.
  • Granite.
  • Marble.
  • Building stone.
129. Placer Mining
  • Placer mining extracts heavy minerals concentrated in loose sediments.
  • Beach sands are an important example.
130. Environmental Impacts of Mining

Mining can cause:

  • Deforestation.
  • Soil erosion.
  • Habitat destruction.
  • Dust pollution.
  • Water pollution.
  • Noise.
  • Waste generation.
  • Land subsidence.
131. Overburden
  • Overburden is the soil and rock covering a mineral deposit.
  • It must be removed in many open-cast mines.
132. Mine Tailings
  • Tailings are finely ground waste materials left after ore processing.
  • They may contain hazardous metals and chemicals.
  • Safe storage is essential.
133. Acid Mine Drainage
  • Sulphide minerals exposed to air and water can produce acidic drainage.
  • Acidic water can dissolve metals and pollute streams.
134. Land Subsidence
  • Underground extraction can create voids.
  • Collapse may cause the ground surface to sink.
  • This is called land subsidence.
135. Mine Reclamation

Mine reclamation may involve:

  • Refilling pits.
  • Regrading slopes.
  • Replacing topsoil.
  • Planting vegetation.
  • Treating polluted water.
136. Minerals and Industrial Location

Industries often develop near mineral deposits to reduce transport costs.

Examples include:

  • Iron and steel near iron ore and coal.
  • Cement near limestone.
  • Aluminium near bauxite and cheap electricity.
137. Iron and Steel Industry Inputs

Major inputs include:

  • Iron ore.
  • Coking coal.
  • Limestone.
  • Manganese.
  • Water.
138. Aluminium Industry Inputs

Major requirements include:

  • Bauxite.
  • Large electricity supply.
  • Transport.
  • Water.
139. Cement Industry Inputs

Major raw materials include:

  • Limestone.
  • Clay.
  • Gypsum.
140. Mineral-Based Industrial Regions

Important mineral-industrial regions include:

  • Chotanagpur.
  • Odisha-Chhattisgarh belt.
  • Eastern Karnataka.
  • Rajasthan mineral belt.
141. Tamil Nadu Mineral Geography — Overview

Important mineral resources of Tamil Nadu include:

  • Lignite.
  • Limestone.
  • Magnesite.
  • Granite.
  • Beach-sand minerals.
  • Graphite in selected areas.
  • Bauxite in limited hill regions.

Energy minerals are covered more fully in the next chapter.

142. Neyveli Lignite
  • Neyveli in Cuddalore district is famous for lignite deposits.
  • It is one of Tamil Nadu's most important mineral-energy locations.
📌 Tamil Nadu Must-Memorise

Neyveli → Lignite → Cuddalore

143. Lignite
  • Lignite is a low-rank brown coal.
  • It contains more moisture and less carbon than higher-rank coal.
  • It is commonly used for thermal power generation near mining areas.
144. Tamil Nadu Limestone
  • Limestone occurs in several parts of Tamil Nadu.
  • Important limestone-bearing districts and belts include areas around:
  • Ariyalur.
  • Tirunelveli.
  • Virudhunagar.
  • Salem and adjoining regions.
🔗 Tamil Nadu Key Link

Ariyalur → Limestone + Cement

145. Ariyalur
  • Ariyalur is well known for limestone deposits.
  • This has supported cement industries in the region.
  • The district is also geologically important for sedimentary and fossil-bearing formations.
📌 Must-Memorise

Ariyalur → Limestone → Cement

146. Salem Magnesite
  • Salem contains major magnesite deposits.
  • Chalk Hills are particularly famous.
📌 Tamil Nadu Must-Memorise

Chalk Hills → Salem → Magnesite

147. Tamil Nadu Graphite
  • Graphite deposits occur in selected parts of Tamil Nadu, including the Sivaganga region.
  • Graphite has industrial and electrochemical uses.
🔗 Tamil Nadu Key Link

Sivaganga → Graphite

148. Tamil Nadu Bauxite
  • Limited bauxite deposits occur in some hill regions.
  • The Shevaroy Hills and Nilgiri-related uplands are associated with lateritic/bauxite occurrences.
149. Shevaroy Hills
  • Shevaroy Hills near Salem contain lateritic formations and bauxite occurrences.
  • Yercaud lies in the Shevaroy Hills.
150. Mineral Sands of Kanyakumari
  • Coastal stretches around Kanyakumari contain heavy mineral sands.
  • Minerals may include:
  • Ilmenite.
  • Garnet.
  • Monazite.
  • Zircon.
151. Mineral Sands of Tirunelveli-Thoothukudi Coast
  • Southern Tamil Nadu's coast contains economically important heavy-mineral placer deposits.
  • These deposits require careful environmental regulation.
152. Tamil Nadu Granite
  • Granite occurs in several districts.
  • It is quarried for:
  • Building stone.
  • Flooring.
  • Decorative use.
  • Export.
153. Mineral Extraction and Tamil Nadu Environment

Important issues include:

  • Quarrying impacts.
  • Sand-mining impacts.
  • Groundwater disturbance.
  • Coastal mineral-sand extraction.
  • Dust pollution.
  • Land degradation.
154. River Sand
  • River sand is a construction material rather than a metallic mineral resource.
  • Excess extraction can:
  • Lower riverbeds.
  • Damage banks.
  • Reduce groundwater recharge.
  • Threaten infrastructure.
155. Beach Sand Mining
  • Beach-sand extraction must account for:
  • Coastal erosion.
  • Dune stability.
  • Marine ecosystems.
  • Radioactive mineral content in selected deposits.
156. Mineral Resource vs Reserve
  • A mineral resource is a concentration with reasonable prospects for eventual economic extraction.
  • A reserve is the economically mineable part demonstrated under specified technical and economic conditions.
📌 TNPSC Advanced Fact

Reserve → Economically Mineable Part of Resource

157. Strategic Minerals
  • Strategic minerals are important for national security, advanced technology and critical industries.
  • Examples can include:
  • Chromium.
  • Rare earth elements.
  • Lithium.
  • Cobalt.
  • Nickel.
  • Certain atomic minerals.
  • Their importance changes with technology.
158. Critical Minerals
  • Critical minerals are minerals whose supply disruption could significantly affect the economy or strategic sectors.
  • Their classification may change with technology, demand and supply chains.
  • Rare earth elements are important examples.
159. Lithium — Importance
  • Lithium is important for rechargeable batteries.
  • It is widely used in:
  • Electric vehicles.
  • Electronics.
  • Energy storage.
  • It is not traditionally one of India's major extensively mined minerals.
160. Cobalt
  • Cobalt is used in:
  • Battery technologies.
  • Superalloys.
  • Specialised industrial applications.
  • Global supply is geographically concentrated.
161. Nickel
  • Nickel is used in:
  • Stainless steel.
  • Alloys.
  • Batteries.
  • It is an important modern industrial mineral.
162. Mineral Mapping

Mineral exploration uses:

  • Geological surveys.
  • Geophysical methods.
  • Geochemical analysis.
  • Remote sensing.
  • Drilling.
163. Geological Survey
  • Geological surveys identify:
  • Rock types.
  • Structures.
  • Mineral occurrences.
  • Potential deposits.
164. Remote Sensing in Mineral Exploration
  • Satellite data can identify:
  • Geological structures.
  • Alteration zones.
  • Lineaments.
  • Surface mineral indicators.
165. Geophysical Exploration

Methods include:

  • Magnetic surveys.
  • Gravity surveys.
  • Electrical methods.
  • Seismic methods.

They help detect subsurface structures.

166. Mineral Resources and Sustainable Development

Sustainable mineral use requires:

  • Efficient extraction.
  • Environmental safeguards.
  • Worker safety.
  • Recycling.
  • Rehabilitation of mined land.
  • Reduced waste.

  • Major mineral classes? → Metallic, non-metallic and energy minerals.
  • What are ferrous minerals? → Minerals associated with iron and steel industries.
  • Major ferrous minerals? → Iron ore, manganese and chromite.

  • Formula of hematite? → Fe₂O₃.

  • Principal ore of tin? → Cassiterite.

  • Important Indian tin region? → Chhattisgarh/Bastar region.
  • Famous historic gold field of Karnataka? → Kolar Gold Fields.

  • Nellore is historically associated with? → Mica.

  • Jaduguda is associated with? → Uranium.
  • Tummalapalle is associated with? → Uranium.
  • Monazite contains important quantities of? → Thorium and rare earth elements.

  • Major heavy beach minerals? → Ilmenite, rutile, monazite, zircon and garnet.
  • Ilmenite is an ore of? → Titanium.
  • Rutile chemical formula? → TiO₂.
  • Which Tamil Nadu coast has important heavy-mineral sands? → Southern coast including Kanyakumari-Tirunelveli-Thoothukudi sectors.

  • Neyveli lies in? → Cuddalore district.
  • Important Tamil Nadu limestone centre? → Ariyalur.
  • Why is Ariyalur important industrially? → Limestone supports cement industry.
  • Important Tamil Nadu graphite region? → Sivaganga.
  • Tamil Nadu district famous for salt pans? → Thoothukudi.
  • What is beneficiation? → Removal of gangue to increase useful mineral concentration.
  • What is open-cast mining? → Surface mining of shallow deposits.
  • What is underground mining? → Extraction through shafts and tunnels.
  • What is overburden? → Soil and rock lying above a mineral deposit.
  • What are tailings? → Waste left after mineral processing.
  • Why should minerals be conserved? → They are finite and take geological time to form.
  • Important mineral-conservation method? → Recycling.
